div.p: To each of those who come in to the common meals the eldest points out the doors: Through these, he says, no word goes out.

The so-called black broth was especially esteemed among them, so that the older men did not need a bit of meat but gave it up to the young men. τοὺς νεανίσκους] τοῖς νεανίσκοις Turnebus It is said that Dionysius, the tyrant of Sicily, for the sake of this bought a Laconian cook and ordered him to prepare it for him, sparing no expense; then, having tasted it and found it disgusting, he spat it out, and the cook said: O king, one must have exercised in the Laconian way and δὲ * bathed in the Eurotas to relish this broth.

The Laconians, having drunk moderately at the common meals, go away without a torch; for they are not permitted to walk by light either on this road or on any other, so that they may become accustomed to travel in darkness and at night boldly and fearlessly.

They learned letters for the sake of their usefulness; but the other kinds of education they banished from the country, men no more than writings.
Their education was aimed at being ruled well, enduring toil, and in battle conquering or dying.
They also went on living without a tunic, receiving one cloak for the year, squalid in their bodies and for the most part abstaining from baths and anointings.

The young men slept together by troop and by herd on pallets which they themselves αὐτοὶ] αὑτοῖς Vit. Lyc. c. 16 brought together, from the reed that grows beside the Eurotas, breaking off its tips with their hands without iron; and in the winter they put underneath and mixed into the pallets the so-called lycophanes, λυκοφάνους *: λυκοφάνας since the material was thought to have something warming in it.

To love boys who were good in soul was permitted; but to consort with them was considered shameful, as loving the body and not the soul; and he who was accused of consorting with one shamefully was deprived of civic rights for life.

It was the custom also for the younger men to be asked by the older where ποῖ *: που they were going and for what; and for the older to rebuke the one who did not answer or who wove excuses. And he who did not rebuke a wrongdoer in his presence was liable to the same penalty as ᾧπερ Herwerdenus: ὥσπερ the wrongdoer; and he who showed resentment, if he was rebuked, was in great disgrace.

If anyone was caught doing wrong, he had to go round in a circle one of the altars in the city.
He sang a censure composed against himself; and this was nothing other than rebuking himself.

And the young were required not only to respect their own fathers and to be obedient to them, but to show regard for all the older men, both making way for them in the streets and giving up their seats to them and keeping quiet in their presence παρόντων X: παριόντων . Therefore each man had authority not, as in the other cities, over his own children and slaves and possessions, but over his own and his neighbour's alike, so that they might share as much as possible and care for things as their own.

If a boy was punished by someone and reported it to his father, it was disgraceful for the father not to lay on him, after hearing it, still more blows; for they trusted one another that, from their ancestral discipline, no one would ἂν Cobetus order anything shameful to the children.

The young also steal whatever of the food they can, learning to make clever attacks on those who are asleep or keep careless watch; and for the one who is caught the penalty is blows and going hungry. For their dinner is scanty, so that, warding off want by their own means, they may be forced to be daring and cunning.

The fare of the common meal was scanty both for these reasons and so that they might become accustomed never to be full, but to be able to go hungry; for in this way they thought they would also be more useful for war, if they were able to toil even without eating, and more self-controlled and more frugal, if they lived for a longer time on small expense.
And to bear ὑποφέρειν M: ἀποφέρειν the lack of relishes, so as to take as food whatever came to hand, they thought made the bodies healthier and well-grown εὐαυξὴ *: εὐεξὴ as a result of the scanty food, believing that, when it was not pressed πιεζόμενον] πιεζόμενον τὸ πνεῦμα? into depth and breadth, it lifts the bodies into height; and that it also made them beautiful; for lean and spare conditions yield to articulation of the limbs, while overfed πολυτρέφους X: πολυεροπους ones resist it because of their weight.

They took no less pains over their melodies and songs; and these had a sting that roused the spirit and called forth an enthusiastic and active impulse. And the diction was simple and unaffected; it contained nothing other than praises of those who had lived nobly and had died for Sparta and are deemed blessed, and censures of those who had played the coward, as living a painful and wretched life; and a promise and a boast about valour fitting for each age.

So, as there were three choruses according to the three ages, and they were formed at the festivals, the chorus of the old men began and sang: We ἄμμες *: ἄμες cf. Bergk. 3 p. 661 once were valiant young men. Then the chorus of the men in their prime said in answer: And we are so now; if you wish, look and see. And the third, that of the boys: And we shall be far mightier.

And their marching rhythms were incitements to courage ἀνδρείαν] ἀνδρείαν ἤσαν? and boldness and contempt for death, and they used them both in dances and to the pipe when leading on against the enemy. For Lycurgus yoked love of music together with training for war, so that the excessively warlike, blended with the melodious, might have concord and harmony; therefore in battles too the king sacrificed beforehand to the Muses, so that the fighters might render their deeds worthy of being told and of glorious remembrance.

If anyone transgressed in any respect the ancient music, they did not allow it; but even Terpander, who was most old-fashioned and the best of the lyre-singers of his time and a praiser of heroic deeds, nevertheless the ephors fined, and they took away his lyre and nailed it up, because he had strung just one string more for the sake of variety of sound; for they approved only the simpler of melodies. And when Timotheus was competing at the Carneia, one of the ephors took a knife and asked him from which of the two sides he should cut off the strings beyond the seven.

Of burials ταφῶν *: τάφων Lycurgus removed all superstition, allowing them to bury the dead in the city and to have the tombs near the sanctuaries. He also did away with the pollutions; he allowed nothing to be buried with the dead, but all alike were to lay the body in a red cloak and olive leaves and wrap it up.
He also removed the inscriptions on the tombs, except for those of men who died in war, and the mournings and lamentations.
They were not allowed to travel abroad, so that they might not share in foreign customs and undisciplined ways of life.
He also introduced expulsions of foreigners, so that those who streamed in might not become teachers of some evil to the citizens.
Whoever of the citizens did not submit to the training of the boys had no share in the rights of the city.

Some said that whoever of the foreigners too submitted to this kind of training in the constitution, in accordance with the intention of Lycurgus, had a share in the portion assigned from the beginning; but selling was not allowed.

They would use the servants of their neighbours as their own, as was the custom, if ever they needed them, and their dogs and horses too, unless the owners required them; and in the country, if anyone found himself short of something and needed it, he would open the owner's store and take away what he needed, and then, having set the seals τὰ σημεῖα] collocaverim post ἀνοίξας. cf. Xen. Reip. Lac. VI 4 on it again, he left it.

In wars they used red cloaks; for on the one hand the colour seemed to them manly, and on the other the blood-red of the hue caused παρεῖχεν *: παρέχειν more fear in the inexperienced; and it is also useful that, if one of them is wounded, it is not easily detected by the enemy, but escapes notice because of the sameness of colour.

Whenever they defeat the enemy by a stratagem, they sacrifice an ox to Ares; whenever in open fight, a cock.
In this way they accustom their leaders to be not only warlike but also skilled in generalship.
To their prayers they add the ability to suffer injustice.
Their prayer is to be given what is fair in return for good deeds, and nothing more.
They worship Aphrodite in arms; and they represent all the gods, female and male, holding spears, as though all possessed the valour of war.

Those who are fond of proverbs also add: Call on Fortune while you put your hand to it,Leutsch. 2 p. 653 meaning that one should call upon the gods while undertaking and doing something oneself, but not otherwise.
They would make the helots drunk and show them to the boys, to turn them away from heavy drinking.
It was their custom not to knock at the outer doors but to shout from outside.
They used strigils not of iron but of reed.
They did not listen to comedies or tragedies, so that they might hear neither in earnest nor in jest those who speak against the laws.
The sacred rites are common to maidens and youths.
The ephors fined Sciraphidas, because he was wronged by many.
They put to death a man who wore sackcloth, because he had put a border on his sackcloth.
They rebuked the young man from the gymnasium, because he knew the road to Pylaea.
Cephisophon, who said that he could speak about any chance subject for the whole day, they expelled, saying that the good speaker must keep his speech equal to the matters in hand.

The boys among them, being flayed with whips throughout the whole day at the altar of Artemis Orthia, often hold out to the point of death, cheerful and proud, competing with one another for victory, as to which of them could endure being beaten longer and more; and the one who prevails is among the most highly esteemed. The contest is called diamastigosis; and it takes place every year.

One of the fine and blessed things which Lycurgus seemed to have provided for the citizens was an abundance of leisure. For they were not allowed to touch any menial craft at all.
And there was no need whatever of money-making, which involves laborious accumulation, or of business, πραγματείας] πραγματείαν Vit. Lyc. c. 24 because he had made wealth entirely unenvied and unhonoured. The helots worked the land for them, paying ἀποφέροντες Turnebus the rent that had been fixed from of old. It was accursed ἐπάρατον] ἀπόρρητον W for anyone to let the land at a higher rent, so that the helots, making a profit, might serve gladly, and the masters might not seek for more.

They were forbidden to be sailors and to fight at sea. Later, however, they did fight at sea, and after gaining mastery of the sea they withdrew from it again, seeing that the characters of the citizens were being corrupted. But they changed again, as in all other things; for when money had been amassed for the Lacedaemonians, those who amassed it were condemned to death. For to Alcamenes and Theopompus, the kings, an oracle was given: Love of money will destroy Sparta. Leutsch. 2 p. 150 Yet Lysander, after conquering the Athenians, brought in much gold and silver, and they accepted it and honoured the man. So long as the city followed the laws of Lycurgus and abided by its oaths, it held the first place in Greece for good order and repute over a period of five hundred years; but as these were transgressed little by little, and greed and love of wealth crept in, the elements of their power also diminished, and because of this the allies were ill-disposed towards them.
Nevertheless, though they were in this state, after the victory of Philip the Macedonian at Chaeronea, when all the Greeks proclaimed him leader both by land and by sea, and in the interval Alexander his son after the destruction of Thebes, the Lacedaemonians alone, although they had an unwalled city and were very few because of their continual wars, and had become much weaker and easy to subdue, preserving some very small sparks of the legislation of Lycurgus, neither joined in the campaigns of these nor of the Macedonian kings in between, nor entered the common council, nor οὔτε *: οὐδὲ paid tribute, until, having utterly disregarded the legislation of Lycurgus, they were ruled as by tyrants by their own citizens, preserving nothing any more of their ancestral discipline; and having become like the others, they put away their former glory and freedom of speech, and passed into slavery, and now they have come under the Romans, like the other Greeks.
